posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.content_md:
Last night I met JohnFP for a night of making holograms. I'm a rank amature who knows only enough to get by, however John graciously invited me into his lab to show me the way. I learned the wonders of DCG and will have a hard time going back to my silver halide setup. DCG has got to be the coolest material I've ever seen! The bright bright holograms, interesting colors, and ease of use are amazing.

In addition I learned some simple tricks of the trade that make life a lot simpler. John also helped me diagnose the characteristics of my new diode laser and we worked to get it up to par for hologram making. I think we got it going well and I hope to start using it tonight.

I really appreciate more experienced holographers sharing their wealth of knowledge and helping little guys like me have more fun in the hobby. John certainly did that for me last night!

With that spirit I think holography will continue to grow and grow. Thanks!

-Jim

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
Jim-

Sounds like a lot of fun and some useful tips as well...

What did you do to your laser to make it work better?

-Tony

posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.content_md:
After watching it mode hop for about an hour. John suggested turning down the power. So I turned the power down by about 1/3 to around 50mW and suddenly the fringes got better contrast and stopped moving. Simple, but effective.

-Jim

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes, but I learned that on this forum. So I have to give credit to the forum. Thanks Forum! I don't even own a diode laser.

Jim, good luck and I am anxious to see some of your work with the new diode.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Jim, I think I found the problems to the blotshies we were getting. The only new thing that was introduced into the process was the blowing off with compressed air just after the alcohol. I elliminated that step and the hologram came out much almost perfectly clear but the big fish moved again. Must fix that. Anyway it seems even though I have a water extractor in the compressed line there is still moisture in there. It explains why there were blotches and the blotches look exaclty like what would be caused by very little dampness in the line. I only have one more 5 x 7 and hope it produces good enough to show. This gives back confidence in my coating method. I still have plenty of 4 x 5's and may shoot a couple of them.

Peace!

posts.content_md:

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Moisture from my compressor was a big problem is spraying laquer onto my guitars. Here was my solution, a bit extreme but it worked very well.

Empty all of the water from the tank with the bleed valve before each use. Run the compressed air through a 25' 3/8" copper coil made from refigeration copper. The coil was imersed into a bucket of ice water. Then I put the air through a filter and a standard air line dryer (available from any automotive paint supplier).

When we were done it was quite dry.
